what_would_change_verdict: Clean underside and trunk-floor photos or a clean specialist PPI would move condition and documentation up materially.
Receipts showing cooling-system replacement, and invoices for the tires and shocks, would raise documentation and lower expected catch-up.
Any subframe cracking, significant rust, or the seller refusing a PPI would move it sharply down.
An explanation for the registration gaps that reveals long storage without maintenance would raise expected catch-up costs.
evidence.mission_note: This fits the enthusiast-bridge brief directly: the main target model in the preferred 3.0i manual form, priced inside the ideal band, and likely easy to resell. Fitness depends on a remote PPI confirming structure and rust, given its snow-belt history.
evidence.rationale: AutoCheck verifies the identity, a clean title, no reported accidents, three owners, and a plausible odometer trail (27,341 mi in 2015, 34,650 now), with the current owner holding the car since 2008. The photos show a visibly clean, apparently stock Sterling Gray roadster with fresh-looking tires and an intact top. The only observed defects are minor bumper scuffs. Maintenance documentation is thin: a single 2015 oil change on record, and unreceipted claims of new tires, battery, rear shocks and inspection. Both model-critical items, rear structure and cooling history, are entirely undocumented. This matters more for a car registered in Erie PA's salt belt since 2003, with registration gaps in 2020 and 2023-2024 that suggest storage periods. The $15,000 ask sits at the fair-value mid, so price neither adds nor removes value, and expected age-related catch-up is real. Whether a PPI can be done in Erie before money moves is not yet established.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller to confirm a PPI is allowed at an Erie-area BMW independent shop, and request underside and trunk-floor photos plus any cooling-system receipts.
